Tracking implemented versus unimplemented features was a mess
Worktrees did not share a compiler cache or build directory
Simulators were shared instead of one per agent or test group
Flaky tests were retried and forgotten instead of flagged and fixed
The UI check used a browser for facts that need no layout, and for untouched screens
Data was keyed by leg numbers, not stable ids; generated files were large and coarse
Most time was spent waiting for CI and tests
The main session relayed every hand-off while agents sat idle

Agents collided on simulators, Chrome, search quota and data files
Ownership of work was unclear
Work died with the session or the laptop
Exists plus green CI was taken to mean correct
How data was verified (simulator, user, online sources) was tribal knowledge, not typed

DISCUSS: CI watcher Stop semantics for timed-out and absent pushes. Now: timed-out (1h) and absent (no run by timeout; interim absent after appear_millis) let Stop pass; unavailable (every job in every run failed with no steps) lets Stop pass; ci-wait exits non-zero for all but passed. Fail closed forever would block a stuck agent with no exit but the owner; failing open waives CI for silent stalls. Agent wall-time budgets (30-60 min) are shorter than the 1h timeout, so a stalled run outlives the agent either way. Unavailable is inferred from job shape only; a billing/spending-limit annotation (gh api check-runs/<job>/annotations) would make it certain at the cost of one call per job. Owner's call.

meta status: one live view of open tasks and their claims, each task's PR and CI state, and each agent's worktree, process and last activity (agents log their worktree when they claim). meta rm <path>...: the only way agents delete files. Deletes only (1) a cargo target dir, or (2) a git worktree or clone whose work is all on a remote: no uncommitted, untracked or stashed changes; every local branch and HEAD on a remote branch; no ignored files other than target dirs. Worktrees go through git worktree remove. Refuses anything in use (an open file or a process cwd inside it). Logs what it removed and the space freed. It becomes the deletion layer of meta gc.

Entity model, part 1, concern (owner, 2026-10-26). A concern is anything noticed that might matter, vague or precise, and is the only entity that carries a ladder rung: 1 identified (text); 2 defined (points at a spec rule); 3 checked or budgeted (a named enforcer: lint, test or CI step); 4 impossible by construction (a type). Moves up and down are events with evidence; a concern never claims a rung its evidence no longer supports. Its division is architecture-and-planning at rungs 1-2, then the owning division at 3-4. Concerns may rest at any rung, but resting is budgeted: a ratchet counts concerns per rung, and the count of low-rung concerns may only go down. Rung is the only typed axis; confidence is not separate, because climbing from rung 1 to 2 already narrows it. Closing: resolved or retired.

Entity model, part 2, spec rule (owner, 2026-10-26). A spec rule is a precise, decided statement and the single source of truth for rung 2 and above: its enforcement is the rung. A rule may settle one or more concerns (a concern at rung 2+ points at its rule and follows the rule's rung), or come straight from an owner decision with no concern behind it. Adding or rewording a rule is owner-only; agents may only propose. Changing a rule's enforcement and rung when a PR adds or removes an enforcer is a normal code change, and reviewers check that it is honest.

Entity model, part 2 (owner, 2026-10-26, revised): 'spec rule' is decomposed into four things. (1) Claim: a typed, checkable property about a subject over a scope; it always carries a rung (2 stated, 3 checked, 4 impossible); adding or rewording a claim is owner-only, and reviewers check enforcement and rung updates. (2) Definition: what a term means; it lives on the type itself (doc string) and carries no rung. (3) Plan: future work; it is a task in the log, not part of the spec. (4) Decision: a logged owner decision (what was decided, why, and which concerns it settles); it may produce claims directly, with no concern behind them. A concern climbs from rung 1 (vague) to a stated claim (2), a checked claim (3), and an impossible violation (4). PR #28 (rung audit of the old rules) is paused as input to the split.

Budget enforcement (owner, 2026-10-26). Budgets are enforced in CI (the local gate where Actions can't run). Per-change budgets: measured fresh by CI. Standing budgets derived from the log (open Criticals, waivers in force, concern backlog): CI folds meta/log read-only on every run; an over-budget standing budget blocks only PRs in its division, but a division whose property all code affects (for example CI performance) blocks every PR that could affect it. Per-task budgets (effort, due): CI finds the PR's task via TaskLinked or the branch, and fails on overspend with no recorded extension; a PR with no task fails. Spend comes from local measurement (heartbeat from transcripts) written to the log; CI trusts it under the honest-mistakes threat model. Machine budgets (CPU, memory, agents, disk) are runtime controls enforced by hooks and leases, not CI; timing budgets are measured only on CI or in the local gate's clean run.

Division domains (owner, 2026-10-26). Only what is measured can be budgeted, so every division declares its domain as typed scopes in policy: crates, paths, CI workflows, tests, plus its implicit items (log entries labelled with it). A child's domain is a strict subset of its parent's. Defaults: all code belongs to features-and-maintenance and, through CI performance (which is always measured, unlike app performance), to performance-and-cost; architecture-and-planning has no code. A budget is a measure over its division's domain (test or workflow wall time, lint findings over crates or paths, open Criticals over items), and a budget whose measure needs a scope the division doesn't declare is refused when the policy is read. A PR is within a budget's reach when its diff touches the domain or its linked task is in the division. Which scope kinds a budget needs depends on the budget; wall-time budgets on tests and workflows are the easiest first case.
